% Please keep the abstract below 300 words
\section*{Abstract}
Before using a decentralized finance contract, an owner signs an ERC-20 approval that lets the contract move its tokens. Graph reputation scores could inform that decision, but an existing method, Adaptive Weighted PageRank (AWP), walks transfers, which record payments, not authorizations. We ask what allowance edges add. On public Arbitrum One logs we compared EndorseRank, PageRank on the latest allowances, with AWP and with the raw degrees that both walks smooth, for 6,483 contracts approved by at least three owners. US-dollar amounts over five tokens and scores from the twelve months before each freeze were defined after a pre-specified analysis in raw token units was complete; we report this revised analysis, applying the pre-specified rules as a re-analysis. Each score agreed most with checks built from its own edges (Kendall $\tau$ 0.560 [95\% CI 0.548, 0.571] for EndorseRank, 0.736 [0.728, 0.744] for AWP). With scores frozen before two three-month windows, neither walk beat its raw degree: AWP ranked later new transfer senders below the transfer in-degree ($\Delta\tau$ $-$0.038 [$-$0.043, $-$0.032] and $-$0.041 [$-$0.047, $-$0.034]), and EndorseRank ranked later new approval pairs below the count of approving owners ($-$0.090 [$-$0.100, $-$0.079] and $-$0.082 [$-$0.090, $-$0.073]), also with activity restarts. These comparisons were chosen after the labels were known. For spenders whose owners are not themselves approved, EndorseRank is a reweighted approval count. On the later liquidation-free close rate of 70 contracts trading on GMX V2, an outcome neither graph contains, the approval count ranked traders above the transfer count ($\Delta\tau$ +0.141; 97.5\% interval [0.026, 0.256]), meeting the pre-specified rule in this re-analysis but not in the pre-specified analysis; the PageRank pair was not resolved (+0.023 [$-$0.071, 0.127]). AWP's graph had 2.21 times as many edges and took 3.21 times as long to solve with the same solver.

\section*{Introduction}

Decentralized finance (DeFi) runs lending, trading and asset management through smart contracts on public blockchains~\cite{schar2021defi,werner2022sok}. Most of these services begin with an authorization: the owner of a token lets a contract move some of it. ERC-20 tokens store such an authorization as an allowance, set by calling \texttt{approve} or by signing an EIP-2612 \texttt{permit}~\cite{vogelsteller2015erc20,lundfall2020permit}. An allowance stays in force until it is spent, replaced or revoked, and most approvals on Ethereum are for unlimited amounts~\cite{wang2022unlimited}, so a malicious contract, or an honest one that is later compromised, can take the owner's entire balance of the approved token. Phishing sites lead users to sign exactly such approvals~\cite{he2023txphishscope}, and the toolkits that do so are sold as a service~\cite{he2025drainer}. Owners, their wallet software and protocols that build on other contracts therefore share one question: which spender contracts deserve an allowance.

Trust in a spender contract forms in a few ways today. Most owners decide when their wallet shows the approval request, and flaws in how wallets display and check approvals leave that moment open to fraud~\cite{adamczyk2025approval}. Code analysis judges a contract by its functions, for instance by flagging functions written for a rug pull~\cite{lin2024crpwarner}. Deployed reputation tools such as Human Passport weigh credentials to decide whether an address belongs to a distinct person~\cite{humanpassportnddocs}, a question about the holder of a key that has no direct counterpart for a contract. None of these uses the public record of what other owners have decided, namely which contracts many owners have authorized.

Graph ranking offers a way to read that record. PageRank gives every node the stationary probability of a damped random walk along directed edges~\cite{page1999pagerank,langville2006pagerank}, and EigenTrust and TrustRank adapt the walk to peer-to-peer trust and to web spam~\cite{kamvar2003eigentrust,gyongyi2004trustrank}. On account-based ledgers the edges have so far been payments. Do and Do apply PageRank and HodgeRank to Ethereum transactions to measure social credit~\cite{do2023hodgerank}. The Adaptive Weighted PageRank (AWP) of Do, Do and Nguyen gives each transfer a weight that rises with its value up to a ceiling and decays logistically with its age, and restarts the walk at addresses that sent recently~\cite{do2023awp}. Its authors check AWP by its agreement with the number and value of the transfers each address receives, statistics of the same transfers that make up its graph.

A transfer shows that value moved, not that the sender vouched for the recipient; routers, market makers, airdrop hunters and wash traders all produce transfers in bulk~\cite{cong2023washtrading,luo2025airdrop}. An allowance records a different act. The holder of the funds names one spender and lets it move up to a stated amount. A new approval for the same owner, spender and token replaces the old one, so the latest allowance summarizes the relation, and approvals are rarer than transfers. An authorization need not express trust. To trade on an exchange a user must first approve its router, whatever the user thinks of it, and a phishing contract collects approvals as an honest one does. We therefore call the allowance edge an authorization and use the name EndorseRank only as the label of a method. Approvals have been used to cluster addresses of one entity~\cite{victor2020clustering}, but we know of no reputation method that ranks contracts on them.

Whether either edge yields the better reputation score for contracts is partly a question of evaluation design, and two habits of the field make it hard to answer. One is to check a score against statistics of its own edges. Such agreement is expected by construction: it speaks to the coherence of the intended construct and not to what else the score can tell~\cite{cronbach1955construct,messick1995validity}. The other is to compare walks only with other walks. A PageRank smooths a local count, and local counts are hard to beat. New links attach preferentially to nodes that already have many~\cite{barabasi1999scaling,newman2001clustering}, degree is a standard baseline in link prediction~\cite{libennowell2007link}, also on Ethereum~\cite{lin2022tracking}, and where degree correlations are weak PageRank is on average proportional to in-degree~\cite{fortunato2008indegree}. A propagated score earns its extra cost only where it beats the count underneath it.

This paper compares the two edge types as reputation scores for smart contracts on Arbitrum One. We score the same contracts with EndorseRank, PageRank on the latest allowances with AWP's edge weights and uniform restarts, with AWP and with the two raw in-degrees, freeze every score before two three-month label windows, and test each score on what happens afterwards. Every scored address holds contract code; externally owned accounts enter the graphs only as owners, senders and recipients. The design was fixed in steps that we report with their commits: an analysis plan before this study extracted any log, and a registration of the second window before this study extracted its logs. The registered analysis that these documents fixed kept amounts in raw token units over every ERC-20 token and scored every event since 1~October~2023. After its results were known, we defined the revised analysis: amounts in US dollars over five widely traded tokens, and every score computed from the twelve months before its freeze. Results report the revised analysis. The rules fixed for the registered analysis are applied to it as a re-analysis, and the registered results are given beside it. There are three contributions.

\begin{itemize}
\item An out-of-window comparison of each walk with the raw degree it smooths, in two windows. Neither the plan nor the registration named these comparisons, and all were computed after the labels were known. Each edge type's scores rank later edges of the same type best, but neither walk ranked them above its own count. AWP ranked later new transfer senders below the transfer in-degree, and EndorseRank ranked later new approval pairs below the count of approving owners, both with the planned uniform restarts and with AWP's activity restarts; the activity restarts narrowed the gap to the count but did not close it.
\item An exact expression for EndorseRank on spenders whose owners receive no approvals: a common constant times one plus the damped owner-normalized in-strength. It holds within 1\% for every such spender, so for most spenders the walk is a reweighted approval count, while the remaining spenders show that multi-hop propagation is present in these graphs.
\item A comparison of the two edge types on an outcome that neither graph contains, the later liquidation avoidance of contracts that trade on the perpetual futures exchange GMX~V2, under rules registered before this study extracted the W1 outcomes (it had extracted the W0 closes but not scored them on liquidation), applied here to the revised scores as a re-analysis. In the primary window the approval count ranked later liquidation avoidance above the transfer count, which meets the registered rule for a count-level lead in this re-analysis but did not in the registered analysis; the PageRank pair was not resolved, and the samples are small.
\end{itemize}

\noindent A companion manuscript by the same authors (unpublished) studies a walk that mixes the two edge types node by node, in the spirit of multilayer ranking~\cite{halu2013multiplex,dedomenico2015ranking}, its ablation, the two decision rules fixed for it in the plan and in the registration, and the Sybil exposure of the allowance walk. Both papers use the same extraction, cohorts, registration and revised analysis, and both report the spender holdout coefficients of the raw degrees, EndorseRank and AWP with their degree contrasts, the closed form of EndorseRank and the solver runtimes. The allowance-against-transfer comparison on trader outcomes (P, Q and rules R1--R3) is reported only here. Both papers report the revised analysis first, with the registered values beside them, and they report the same values for both analyses. On the same W1 trader cohort and liquidation-free close rate the companion reports only the contrasts of the mixed walk with its single-layer walks or AWP that its own registered rule names; here the two single-layer walks enter only through the registered pairs of the trader comparison.

\subsection*{Related work}

\textit{On-chain reputation and risk.} Besides the two PageRank studies above~\cite{do2023hodgerank,do2023awp}, RiskProp rates Ethereum accounts by propagating risk through the transaction network~\cite{lin2025riskprop}, and network embeddings of the transaction graph help detect phishing addresses~\cite{wu2022phishers}. Surveys of blockchain trust and reputation systems find explicit ratings and transfer activity to be the usual signals~\cite{bellini2020trust,almasoud2020reputation}. Decentralized credit scoring combines ledger records with prospect theory~\cite{hassija2020lending} or machine learning~\cite{kotb2023credit}, and legal scholarship warns that such scores can become as opaque as the models they would replace~\cite{packin2024credit}. A study of the ERC-20 transfer network finds that externally owned accounts and smart contracts follow different statistical patterns~\cite{mukhia2026erc20}, one reason to score contracts as a population of their own. These approaches score accounts by what they send and receive; none ranks contracts by the allowances that owners grant them.

\textit{Trust propagation and its weak points.} HITS separates hubs from authorities~\cite{kleinberg1999hits}. EigenTrust normalizes local trust so that no peer can raise its own standing at will~\cite{kamvar2003eigentrust}, and TrustRank lets trust flow outward from a vetted seed set~\cite{gyongyi2004trustrank}. Under uniform teleportation that protection is weaker: alliances of link farms lift a target's PageRank~\cite{gyongyi2005alliances}, and symmetric reputation functions such as PageRank cannot be Sybil-proof~\cite{cheng2005sybilproof}. Both results apply to allowance graphs, where an approval costs a transaction fee and locks no tokens, and where whoever deploys a contract can create owner addresses at almost no cost~\cite{douceur2002sybil}.

\textit{Approvals.} EIP-20 specifies the allowance, and EIP-2612 extends it to signed approvals~\cite{vogelsteller2015erc20,lundfall2020permit}. Wang et al.\ measure how common unlimited approvals are and how much value they expose~\cite{wang2022unlimited}. Studies of transaction-based phishing and of drainer services show how attackers obtain approvals~\cite{he2023txphishscope,he2025drainer}, and Adamczyk dissects an approval-based fraud scheme and the wallet weaknesses it uses~\cite{adamczyk2025approval}. Victor's self-authorization heuristic reads approvals as links between addresses of one entity~\cite{victor2020clustering}.

\textit{Baselines and evaluation.} Degree is the natural benchmark for predicting new links~\cite{libennowell2007link,lin2022tracking}, and PageRank often behaves like a monotone function of in-degree~\cite{fortunato2008indegree}. Construct validity separates what a score measures from its agreement with checks built into it~\cite{cronbach1955construct}. Writing an analysis down before its data are examined limits analytic flexibility~\cite{nosek2018preregistration}; where we could, we fixed each rule before this study extracted the data that judge it, and we state for each comparison when it was fixed.

\section*{Materials and methods}

\subsection*{Data and cohorts}

All events come from Arbitrum One, an optimistic rollup on Ethereum~\cite{kalodner2018arbitrum}, read from the public BigQuery table \texttt{goog\_blockchain\_arbitrum\_one\_us.logs} (project \texttt{bigquery-public-data}). The extraction covers 1~October~2023 through 30~June~2026 and, for the labels of the second window, July to September~2026. Every score reported here is computed from the twelve months before its freeze, its score window: from 1~July~2025 to 30~June~2026 (the end, 23:59:59~UTC, is written $\Tobs$) for the same-window evaluation and the second window, and from 1~April~2025 to 31~March~2026 for the first. A window of one year describes each contract by its activity in the year before the freeze and gives both freezes windows of equal length. We read ERC-20 \texttt{Approval} and \texttt{Transfer} logs with exactly three topics, which leaves out the ERC-721 logs that share their signatures, and the \texttt{PositionDecrease} events of GMX~V2, a perpetual futures exchange on Arbitrum One~\cite{gmxnddocs}. S1 Text gives the topics, decoded fields, label formulas and queries.

\textit{Contracts.} We treat an address as a contract if \texttt{eth\_getCode} at a pinned block returns non-empty code; an address with empty code, or with code that is only an EIP-7702 delegation designator~\cite{buterin2024eip7702}, is an externally owned account (EOA). The analysis plan's candidate spenders, every address that received a non-zero approval from at least three distinct owners in the extracted logs up to $\Tobs$, numbered 29,022. At block 513,216,506 (9~October~2026) 27,844 of them held contract code, 1,121 held none and 57 held a delegation designator. Only contracts are scored or evaluated. EOAs, which may belong to individuals, are present only as owners, senders and recipients and are never ranked or reported.

\textit{Tokens and prices.} Amounts of different tokens can be added only after they are valued in one unit. We keep the approvals and transfers of five tokens, WETH, USDC, USDT0, ARB and WBTC, and value every amount in US dollars at DefiLlama's daily closing price~\cite{defillamanddocs}. We admitted a token if Chainlink's list of data feeds on Arbitrum One shows a market-price feed rated low or medium market risk for the token, for the asset it wraps one to one, or for the Ethereum token of which it is the canonical-bridge copy~\cite{chainlinknddatafeeds}, and if the token occurs in the data. Of the 133 tokens that the list maps to Arbitrum One addresses, 64 qualified and 46 of these have a daily price; the five kept are those with the most rows in the score window of $\Tobs$, together 79.40\% of the rows of all tokens there. Every day of the score and label windows has a price for each of the five tokens. Checked against Chainlink answers read on the chain for 20 of these days per token, the DefiLlama prices were off by a median of 0.010\% to 0.056\% per token, with a largest gap of 0.24\%. A transfer is valued at the price of its day and a latest allowance at the price of the anchor's day, because the edge represents the authorization that holds at the anchor. Keeping five tokens also removes the logs that spam and address-poisoning tokens can emit in the name of owners who never approved or paid anyone. Native ether moves without \texttt{Transfer} logs and enters the graphs only as WETH.

\textit{Cohorts.} The matched cohort consists of the 6,483 contracts that at least three distinct owners approved, with a non-zero amount of one of the five tokens, in the score window of $\Tobs$; they are the part of the plan's 27,844 contracts that meets the same rule on the five tokens within that window. The first freeze has a cohort of its own, drawn by the same rule from its score window so that no event after the freeze chooses it: 6,343 contracts, 5,383 of which are also in the matched cohort. The extraction kept the events with a contract of the plan's cohort at one end: approvals in which it is owner or spender, and non-zero transfers in which it is sender or recipient. Each freeze uses those of its own cohort in its score window and label window. The graphs are therefore one-hop neighbourhoods of the cohort, and a path of two or more edges can exist only through cohort contracts that both grant and receive approvals. Of the ego events of the plan's cohort in the score window of $\Tobs$, the analysis keeps 85,986,562 approvals and 442,722,039 transfers, 63.3\% and 76.2\%. A spender cohort holds, at each freeze, every contract approved inside the score window with an allowance of one of the five tokens that is still positive at the freeze: 7,914 contracts at the first freeze, of 7,962 such spenders, and 7,960 at the second. It includes contracts outside the cohort that a cohort contract had approved. A trader cohort holds the GMX~V2 accounts with contract code that appear as a node of either graph at the freeze and close three or more positions in the label window: 87 contracts in the first window and 70 in the second. From October~2023 to June~2026 contract accounts made 133,685 GMX~V2 closes, including 6,473 liquidations; from July to September~2026 they made 6,805, including 182 liquidations. Few contract accounts traded in the label windows, so every trader result rests on few contracts. S1 Table summarizes windows, cohorts, graphs and amounts.

\textit{Windows.} Window W0 freezes the scores at $t_1=$ 31~March~2026, 23:59:59~UTC, using the events of its score window from 1~April~2025, and counts its labels over April, May and June 2026. Window W1 freezes them at $\Tobs$, so its scores are those of the same-window evaluation, and counts its labels over July, August and September 2026. The two score windows overlap from July~2025 to March~2026, and W1's score window contains W0's label window, so the windows are not independent samples.

\subsection*{Order of the analyses and what was fixed when}

The comparisons were fixed at different times relative to the data, so we state the order of events (times in UTC; S1 File reproduces the plan and the registration).
\begin{itemize}
\item At 13:41:27 on 9~October~2026 an analysis plan and a versioned configuration were committed to the authors' public repository (commit \texttt{43d8045}); no log of this study had yet been extracted. Together they fixed the windows, the cohort and account-type rules, every score with its damping, decay, value transform and restart rule, EndorseRank's uniform restarts with the activity-restart variant to be reported beside it, the raw degrees, the same-window checks, the W0 labels and the statistics. Amounts were to stay in raw token base units over every ERC-20 token, and every score was to use every extracted event from 1~October~2023 up to its freeze. The plan named no comparison of a PageRank with its raw degree.
\item The logs from 1~October~2023 to 30~June~2026 were extracted, and the same-window and W0 results of this registered analysis were computed.
\item At 16:49:32 the registration of W1 was committed (commit \texttt{0d3a057}), once the W0 results were in, and before this study extracted any July--September log. Its section on outcomes built from neither edge type fixed the trader cohort and labels, four pairs of an allowance-side and a transfer-side score, the decision contrasts P and Q, the stratification, the recipient comparison, the influence check and rules R1--R3 with the wording of each conclusion. The extraction script refuses to run without the committed registration; it recorded the registration's SHA-256 hash and started at 16:49:33, and it created the query for the July--September logs at 16:49:40, eight seconds after the commit. At that point no score of this study had been set against a liquidation label of the traders in either window, but an exploratory run had scored the W0 trader contracts on the four profit labels.
\item The July--September logs were extracted and the registered evaluation was run. The comparisons of EndorseRank's activity variant with the approval count, and of EndorseRank with AWP in W1, were computed afterwards. The results of the registered analysis, with these later comparisons, were committed in \texttt{8d8b568}.
\item After all registered results were known, the revised analysis was defined. In raw base units AWP's value weight was within $10^{-4}$ of one for almost every amount, so the amount played no part in EndorseRank or AWP; the companion's amount-weighted layers added base units of tokens whose scales differ by twelve orders of magnitude; and every ERC-20 contract counted, including tokens that emit logs in the name of owners who took no part. The revised analysis values amounts in US dollars over five tokens, sets the slopes of the value weight and a cap on allowances in the amount-weighted allowance layer, and computes every score from the twelve months before its freeze, with the cohort of each freeze drawn from its own score window. Its results, computed at code revision \texttt{0a94215}, were published with the documents that define it in commit \texttt{950a7a4}.
\end{itemize}
\noindent The revised analysis is the one reported in Results. Because its amounts, tokens and score windows were chosen once the registered results were known, no revised result counts as a registered one: rules R1--R3 are applied to it with their registered thresholds and wording, as a re-analysis, and the Results subsection ``The registered analysis'' sets the registered values beside the revised ones. Every comparison of a PageRank with its raw degree, in both analyses, was computed after the labels of its window were known. The closed form was derived to account for the computed scores and tests nothing.

\subsection*{Scores}

\subsubsection*{Weighted PageRank}
Every score is computed by one weighted PageRank solver. With edge weights $w(u,v)$, out-strength $o(u)=\sum_v w(u,v)$ and a restart distribution $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ over the node set $V$, the iteration is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:pagerank}
\mathbf{r}^{(t+1)} = (1-d)\,\boldsymbol{\pi} + d\,P^{\top}\mathbf{r}^{(t)} + d\,\Bigl(\sum_{u:\,o(u)=0} r^{(t)}_u\Bigr)\boldsymbol{\pi},
\qquad
P_{uv}=\frac{w(u,v)}{o(u)}\ \text{if } o(u)>0,
\end{equation}
where the rows of dangling nodes ($o(u)=0$) are zero, so that the last term returns their mass through $\boldsymbol{\pi}$. The damping factor is $d=0.85$; the iteration starts from the uniform vector and stops once the $L_1$ change falls below $10^{-8}$ or after 300 iterations. A cohort contract that a graph does not contain scores zero under that graph's methods; the plan fixed keeping it as an isolated node as a sensitivity analysis.

\subsubsection*{AWP on transfers}
Following Do, Do and Nguyen~\cite{do2023awp}, a transfer $e$ worth $x_e$ US dollars, made $\Delta t_e$ days before the anchor, adds $\sigma(\Delta t_e)\,V(x_e)$ to the edge from its sender to its recipient, with
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:weights}
\sigma(\Delta t)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\bigl(k(\Delta t-t_0)\bigr)},
\qquad
V(z)=\frac{2}{1+e^{-bz}}-1,
\qquad
b=\frac{\ln 3}{m},
\end{equation}
so that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:awp-weight}
w_T(u,v)=\sum_{e:\,u\to v}\sigma(\Delta t_e)\,V(x_e),
\qquad
\pi_u\propto X_u=\sum_{v\neq u}\ \max_{e:\,u\to v}\sigma(\Delta t_e).
\end{equation}
The restart weight $X_u$, which the authors call activeness, sums the time weight of $u$'s latest transfer to each address it has paid, so an address that never pays another receives no restart mass. The paper gives no parameter values. The plan fixed $k=0.01$ and $t_0=180$ days. The anchor of the decay is the freeze date of each window, so the ages in a score window run from zero to 365 days and the time weight falls from $\sigma(0)=0.858$ through $\sigma(90)=0.711$ and $\sigma(182)=0.495$ to $\sigma(365)=0.136$ for an event on the window's first day. The slope is set from the median amount: $m_T=170$ dollars, the median transfer in the W0 score window rounded to two significant digits, so a transfer of the median amount has value weight one half, one of twice that amount 0.8 and one of half of it 0.27.

\subsubsection*{EndorseRank on latest allowances}
EndorseRank puts AWP's weights on the allowance graph. For each token, owner and spender only the most recent \texttt{Approval} in the score window is kept, in block and log order, and a latest value of zero deletes the entry. An edge $u\to v$ means that owner $u$ holds a positive latest allowance for spender $v$ on at least one token, and its weight is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:er-weight}
w_A(u,v)=\sum_{\mathrm{token}}\sigma\bigl(\Delta t^{\star}(u,v,\mathrm{token})\bigr)\,V\bigl(a^{\star}(u,v,\mathrm{token})\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $a^{\star}$ is the latest allowance in US dollars and $\Delta t^{\star}$ the age of the approval that set it. The slope uses $m_A=100$ dollars, the median finite latest allowance at $t_1$, likewise rounded, so an allowance of a few hundred dollars weighs nearly as much as an unlimited one, and no allowance weighs more than one. EndorseRank restarts uniformly. Carrying AWP's rule over to allowances would send the walk back to owners in proportion to how many spenders each has approved, discounted by the age of each latest approval; that rewards the granting of approvals, while EndorseRank is meant to rank the contracts that receive them. The plan therefore fixed uniform restarts and named the variant with activity restarts as a score to report beside EndorseRank. The weight describes the latest approval, its amount and its time, and not what remains of the allowance at the anchor. Only approvals inside the score window are read, so an allowance still in force at the freeze but last approved before the window opened has no edge, and the graph records what owners authorized during that year; spending through \texttt{transferFrom} does not lower the recorded amount of a finite allowance; and an owner that approves an allowance manager such as Uniswap's Permit2 is linked to the manager, not to the contracts the manager authorizes in turn (S1 Text).

\subsubsection*{Raw degrees and amount-weighted layers}
The in-approve degree of a contract is the number of distinct owners that hold a positive latest allowance for it, and its transfer in-degree is the number of distinct other addresses that have sent it a transfer, both counted at the freeze on the events of the score window:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:degrees}
k_A(v)=\bigl|\{u : a^{\star}(u,v,\cdot)>0\}\bigr|,
\qquad
k_T(v)=\bigl|\{u\neq v : u \text{ sent a transfer to } v\}\bigr|.
\end{equation}
Each count is the local statistic that one of the two PageRanks smooths, and out of window each serves as the baseline that its PageRank has to beat. The registered trader comparison also sets against each other the two single-layer end points of the companion's mixed walk, written C-PR($\lambda{=}1$) and C-PR($\lambda{=}0$). Each walks one edge type with uniform restarts and with amounts in dollars, not the bounded weight $V$: the allowance layer sums $\min(a^{\star},U)$ over tokens, with $U=19{,}000$ dollars, the 99th percentile of single transfers in the W0 score window, and the transfer layer sums $x_e\,\sigma(\Delta t_e)$ over transfers. Since the constants $m_T$, $m_A$ and $U$ come from the W0 score window, no label window enters them.

\subsection*{Checks and labels}

\textit{Same-window checks.} Each score is compared on the matched cohort with three families of local statistics computed over the score window of $\Tobs$~\cite{do2023awp}. The transfer family holds a contract's in-degree and the summed dollar value of its inbound transfers. The allowance family holds its in-approve degree and the summed capped value of the allowances it holds. The Sybil-stability family holds the ratio of distinct inbound counterparties to inbound transfers, the span between its first and last transfer and its number of active months. The first two families come from the same events as the two graphs, so a score's agreement with the family of its own edges is an intended-construct check, partly built in, and not evidence of predictive power.

\textit{Spender labels.} Two counts are taken in each label window, one per construct. New approval pairs counts the owners that give the spender a positive approval in the window while their pair held no positive latest allowance at the freeze. New transfer senders counts the distinct addresses that send the spender a transfer in the window and had sent it none since the score window opened, self-transfers excluded. Both count events of the five tokens only, and both count edges of the kinds that build the graphs, so agreement with them shows persistence of a construct, not anticipation of a different outcome. Both labels are sparse. Only 1,732 of the 7,914 W0 spenders (21.9\%) gained any new approval pair over the three months, and 1,422 (18.0\%) any new sender.

\textit{Trader labels.} Six outcomes are computed from each trader contract's GMX~V2 closes in the label window (formulas in S1 Text). A close is one \texttt{PositionDecrease} event, so partial closes count, and it counts as a liquidation if the event carries the liquidation order type or was emitted by the exchange's liquidation handler. The liquidation-free close rate (LFCR), the primary label, is one minus the share of closes that ended in liquidation, and the no-liquidation flag is one when none did. The number of profitable closes and the realized gain, the sum of positive profits, grow with the amount of trading; the profitable share and the non-loss share of closes do not. A liquidated close counts as neither profitable nor losing, so it lowers the profitable share but raises the non-loss share. The six outcomes come from the exchange's position events and not from the edges of either graph, and in that sense we call them outcomes built from neither edge type. They are not wholly separate from the transfer layer: the exchange settles collateral and profits in ERC-20 tokens, so payouts made before the freeze can appear as transfers in the pre-freeze graph. A liquidation closes a leveraged position whose collateral no longer covers its losses~\cite{perez2021liquidations}. It is not a credit default, since the position is settled against the trader's own collateral, but among the outcomes in these data it comes nearest to a counterparty failing to cover its obligations.

\subsection*{Comparison on outcomes built from neither edge type}

The registration of W1 sets allowance-side scores against transfer-side scores in four pairs: the in-approve degree against the transfer in-degree; EndorseRank with activity restarts against AWP, which share the form of their edge weights and their restart rule and differ in the edge type; EndorseRank against AWP; and C-PR($\lambda{=}1$) against C-PR($\lambda{=}0$). C-PR($\lambda{=}0$) minus AWP is reported to isolate AWP's weights and restarts. All six labels are reported. W1 is the primary window and W0 the secondary one. Two contrasts on LFCR in W1 decide: P (in-approve degree minus transfer in-degree) and Q (EndorseRank with activity restarts minus AWP), both judged on Bonferroni 97.5\% intervals. Three rules were registered.
\begin{itemize}
\item R1, a count-level lead on liquidation avoidance, holds if the 97.5\% interval of P lies above zero in W1, the 95\% interval of P stratified by the number of closes lies above zero in W1, and P is positive in W0.
\item R2, a PageRank-level lead, holds if the 97.5\% interval of Q lies above zero in W1 and Q is positive in W0.
\item R3 applies if, in W1, P on the profitable share or on the non-loss share has a 95\% interval entirely below zero; the allowance signal is then taken to be specific to avoiding liquidation.
\end{itemize}
The registration also fixed the wording of each conclusion. If R1 holds, ``the approval count at the freeze ranked contract traders above the transfer count on later liquidation avoidance'', and if it fails, there is ``no count-level lead of allowance over transfer on later liquidation avoidance''; if R2 fails, ``the PageRank versions are not resolved''; and if R3 applies, ``the signal concerns forced-liquidation avoidance, not trading success''. Traders that held at least one approval at the freeze, which we call recipients, are set against all other traders on every label, and as an influence check P is recomputed without the ten recipients with the most approving owners. The evaluation code committed with the registration also computes EndorseRank minus the in-approve degree and the coefficient of every single score, which the registration document does not name.

\subsection*{Statistical analysis}

Agreement between a score and a check or label is measured by Kendall's rank correlation~\cite{kendall1938rank} in its tie-corrected form $\tau_b$, on raw scores and raw values, so that tied scores stay tied. We write $\tau(a)$ for the coefficient of score $a$ and $\dt=\tau(a)-\tau(b)$ for a paired contrast. Uncertainty comes from a paired bootstrap over contracts~\cite{efron1979bootstrap} with percentile intervals~\cite{diciccio1996bootstrap}: the evaluated cohort is resampled with replacement, and one matrix of resample indices is shared by every score, so a contrast keeps the covariance of its two coefficients. The same window and the spender holdouts use 400 resamples with seed 42, and the trader comparison 2,000 with the same seed. With 400 resamples each interval end carries a Monte Carlo error of about 0.13 bootstrap standard errors. Only P and Q in W1 are judged on Bonferroni 97.5\% intervals; every other interval is unadjusted. A contrast is described as a difference when its interval excludes zero. The intervals treat contracts as independent and the graphs, and so the scores, as fixed, although spenders share owners. No $p$-values are reported, and no causal claim is made.

Two properties of the data bear on the comparisons. The raw degrees are integer counts with many ties, whereas EndorseRank leaves few (Results), so part of a gap between a count and a walk may reflect how $\tau_b$ treats ties rather than information. And a trader with more closes has more chances to be liquidated at least once, so for the traders $\tau_b$ is also calculated within strata of 3--4, 5--9, 10--24 and at least 25 closes in the label window and averaged with weights proportional to the number of contract pairs per stratum. The number of closes is measured after the freeze, so the stratification is descriptive.

\subsection*{Closed-form check and runtime}

The closed form derived in Results was checked against EndorseRank as computed on the allowance graphs at both freezes: for every spender of the checked set the pipeline compares the computed score with the closed form and records whether it lies within 1\%. Runtime covers one solver call on prebuilt edge lists, with matrix assembly and power iteration: one untimed warm-up and five timed runs, under identical settings, of one Python implementation (SciPy sparse matrices, NumPy power iteration) on a machine with an Intel Core Ultra~9 185H processor and 64~GB of memory under Windows~11 (Python~3.11.9, NumPy~2.3.2, SciPy~1.16.1).

\subsection*{Ethics statement}

This study used only publicly available blockchain data and public token prices and involved no human participants. The scored addresses are contracts; no externally owned account is scored or reported, no attempt was made to link any address to a real-world identity, and only aggregate statistics are reported. \section*{Results}

\subsection*{Graph structure and coverage}

On the same contracts the two graphs differ in size and shape (Table~\ref{tab1}). The allowance graph at $\Tobs$ holds 3,808,949 edges among 2,514,846 nodes; the transfer graph holds 8,426,124 edges among 3,603,300 nodes, 2.21 times as many edges. A revoked allowance removes its edge, while any pair that exchanged a transfer at some point in the window keeps a transfer edge. Owners holding a positive allowance account for 2,508,872 of the allowance graph's nodes, so that graph is a large fan of owners pointing at comparatively few spenders, and 2,084,669 of its 4,185,287 positive latest allowances (49.8\%) are unlimited. Coverage of the cohort also differs. Of the 6,483 cohort contracts, 191 lie outside the allowance graph, because every allowance set in the window to them or by them was zero at $\Tobs$; 1,192 lie outside the transfer graph, and 30 outside both. EndorseRank leaves few ties among the cohort (5,641 distinct scores; 0.20\% of contract pairs tied) and AWP somewhat more (5,292 distinct scores; 3.38\% of pairs tied), most of them among the contracts that score zero.

\subsection*{Each score agrees most with the checks of its own edges}

In the same window each score follows the edges it walks on (Table~\ref{tab2}). On the allowance family EndorseRank reaches $\tau=0.560$ $[0.548,0.571]$ against $0.226$ $[0.210,0.245]$ for AWP; on the transfer family AWP reaches $0.736$ $[0.728,0.744]$ against $0.196$ $[0.180,0.216]$ for EndorseRank. The paired differences are $\dt=+0.333$ $[0.311,0.354]$ (EndorseRank minus AWP, allowance family) and $+0.539$ $[0.518,0.560]$ (AWP minus EndorseRank, transfer family). This is the pattern an intended-construct check expects, and part of it is built in: EndorseRank agrees most with the in-approve degree ($0.650$ $[0.639,0.661]$), the count it smooths. With dollar amounts, AWP's agreement with the value of inbound transfers ($0.730$ $[0.720,0.740]$) comes close to its agreement with the number of distinct senders ($0.742$ $[0.732,0.752]$), as its value weight intends. On the Sybil-stability family, which averages transfer-based measures of how long and how evenly a contract has received transfers, AWP reaches $0.419$ $[0.408,0.434]$ and EndorseRank only $0.026$ $[0.012,0.041]$. With activity restarts EndorseRank agrees more with its own family ($0.601$ $[0.590,0.613]$) and with the transfer family ($0.251$ $[0.233,0.271]$), because its restarts then land mostly on the owners that grant the most approvals, so a spender's score depends on how busy its owners are and not only on how many it has.

The two walks order the contracts differently. Their rankings agree at $\tau_b=0.199$ $[0.181,0.221]$: both scores order 96.4\% of the 21,011,403 pairs of cohort contracts, and they disagree on the direction for 39.8\% of those. Keeping the contracts outside a graph as isolated nodes, which the plan fixed as a sensitivity analysis, changes this agreement at none of the three reported decimals. A protocol that relies on a transfer-based score cannot assume that its ordering of contracts survives a switch to an allowance-based one.

\subsection*{Out of window, each edge type ranks later edges of its own type}

Table~\ref{tab3} sets every score frozen at each date against the two spender labels. As persistence would lead one to expect, the edge type decides which label a score ranks best. In W0 the in-approve degree ranks new approval pairs at $\tau=0.392$ $[0.377,0.406]$, EndorseRank at $0.303$ $[0.287,0.319]$ and its activity variant at $0.332$ $[0.315,0.347]$, while the transfer in-degree ($0.203$ $[0.183,0.224]$) and AWP ($0.196$ $[0.178,0.213]$) stay lower. On new transfer senders the order reverses: the transfer in-degree reaches $0.447$ $[0.435,0.459]$ and AWP $0.409$ $[0.396,0.421]$, against $0.272$ $[0.257,0.286]$ for EndorseRank. EndorseRank minus AWP is $\dt=+0.107$ $[0.086,0.130]$ on new approval pairs and $-0.138$ $[-0.151,-0.123]$ on new senders. W1 repeats the pattern (Table~\ref{tab3}): EndorseRank minus AWP is $+0.142$ $[0.119,0.164]$ on new approval pairs and $-0.139$ $[-0.154,-0.125]$ on new senders. In both windows the count of the same edge type leads its label.

\subsection*{Neither walk beats the raw degree it smooths}

Against the raw degree it smooths, on the label of its own edge type, neither walk does better (Fig~\ref{fig1}A). On later new transfer senders AWP trails the transfer in-degree by $\dt=-0.038$ $[-0.043,-0.032]$ in W0 and $-0.041$ $[-0.047,-0.034]$ in W1. So on the transfer side AWP's walk, with its time and value weights and its restarts at active senders, ranked these arrivals below the count of distinct senders. EndorseRank, restarting uniformly as the plan fixed, trails the in-approve degree on later new approval pairs by $-0.090$ $[-0.100,-0.079]$ in W0 and $-0.082$ $[-0.090,-0.073]$ in W1. On both sides the count of distinct counterparties was the better predictor. Neither the plan nor the registration document named any of these contrasts. In the registered analysis the evaluation code committed with the registration, before this study extracted the W1 logs, already contained the two W1 contrasts of EndorseRank and AWP with their degrees; the W0 contrasts, the activity-variant contrasts and every contrast of the revised analysis were chosen and computed after the labels were known.

With AWP's activity restarts EndorseRank ranks new approval pairs above its uniformly restarted form in both windows, by $+0.029$ $[0.023,0.037]$ in W0 and $+0.035$ $[0.029,0.042]$ in W1, but it still falls below the in-approve degree, by $-0.060$ $[-0.070,-0.052]$ and $-0.046$ $[-0.055,-0.038]$. The two variants differ in nothing but where the walk restarts, so on these labels the activity restarts narrow the walk's gap to the count without closing it. These comparisons, too, were made after the labels of each window were known.

Coverage does not explain the degree comparisons. AWP gives zero to the 1,342 W0 spenders that had no transfer edge before the freeze, about one in six. These spenders went on to gain new approval pairs more often than the others (26.7\% against 20.9\%) but hardly ever gained a new sender (1.4\% against 21.3\%). Restricted to the 6,489 spenders with an inbound transfer from another address before the freeze, a subset chosen after the results were known, both degree comparisons keep their signs: AWP minus the transfer in-degree is $-0.051$ $[-0.059,-0.043]$ on new senders, and EndorseRank minus the in-approve degree is $-0.087$ $[-0.096,-0.078]$ on new approval pairs. Coverage does explain part of the comparison across edge types: on that subset AWP ranks new approval pairs at $0.328$ $[0.312,0.343]$, above EndorseRank ($0.299$ $[0.283,0.315]$) and below the in-approve degree ($0.387$ $[0.370,0.402]$), with no paired contrast computed; EndorseRank's advantage over AWP on new approval pairs therefore comes from the spenders outside that subset, among them the 1,342 that AWP scores zero. Ties may play a part on both sides. The in-approve degree and the transfer in-degree are heavily tied integer counts, whereas EndorseRank gives 7,368 distinct scores to the 7,914 W0 spenders and ties 0.058\% of their pairs, and AWP gives 1,342 of them the same score of zero and ties 2.87\% of their pairs; $\tau_b$ treats these differently, and no tie-robust comparison was made.

Two further labels, which the plan did not name, were computed on the W0 spenders: revocations, the owners of a positive allowance at the freeze that set it to zero in the label window, and drained owners, a heuristic count of owners whose new approval was followed within hours by an outgoing transfer of the same token (S1 Text). Every score ranks both positively. Revocations follow the in-approve degree most closely ($0.384$ $[0.366,0.399]$) and the transfer in-degree least ($0.186$ $[0.167,0.209]$); for drained owners the coefficients run from $0.162$ $[0.143,0.183]$ for the transfer in-degree to $0.341$ $[0.325,0.356]$ for EndorseRank with activity restarts. A contract that owners trusted more should lose approvals less often, not more, so these counts fit the volume of owner activity rather than endorsement, and neither is offered as evidence.

\subsection*{What EndorseRank computes on depth-one spenders}

The one-hop extraction makes most nodes of the allowance graph either pure owners or pure spenders. A cohort contract can be both, since it can receive approvals and approve other contracts, so the graph also has longer paths. For a spender whose owners receive no approvals, EndorseRank can be written out.

\textit{Observation.} Let PageRank follow \Eq{eq:pagerank} with damping $d$ and uniform restarts, $\pi_u=1/|V|$, and let $r_D$ be the total score of the dangling nodes. Every node without in-edges then has the common score
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:c}
c=\frac{1-d+d\,r_D}{|V|},
\end{equation}
and a node $v$ none of whose in-neighbors has an in-edge of its own scores
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:closed-form}
r_v=c\,\bigl(1+d\,\delta(v)\bigr),
\qquad
\delta(v)=\sum_{u}\frac{w(u,v)}{o(u)}.
\end{equation}
Here $\delta(v)$ is the owner-normalized in-strength of $v$: each owner $u$ contributes the share of its own approval weight that goes to $v$, so an owner that approves many spenders adds little to each of them.

\textit{Derivation.} At the fixed point of \Eq{eq:pagerank} every node $v$ receives $(1-d)/|V|$ from teleportation and $d\,r_D/|V|$ from the dangling rows, together $c$, plus $d\sum_u r_u\,w(u,v)/o(u)$ from its in-neighbors. A node without in-edges receives only $c$. If every in-neighbor $u$ of $v$ is such a node, substituting $r_u=c$ gives \Eq{eq:closed-form}.

The expression is a one-step expansion of the fixed point rather than a closed form in the strict sense, because $c$ depends on $r_D$, which the whole score vector determines; but $c$ is common to all spenders it covers, so EndorseRank orders those spenders exactly as $\delta(v)$ does. It describes the computed scores (Table~\ref{tab1}). In the graph at $\Tobs$ every node without in-edges has the same score, $c=1.93\times10^{-7}$, up to floating-point error. Among the 6,224 cohort spenders, the 5,232 of depth one all lie within 1\% of \Eq{eq:closed-form}; among the remaining 992, whose owners include at least one approved address, only 21.9\% do, which makes 87.5\% over all spenders. On the graph at $t_1$, 5,092 of the 7,905 W0 spenders with an allowance in-edge have depth one, again all within 1\%, and 70.8\% of these W0 spenders lie within 1\%. The W0 spender cohort has more deeper spenders partly because it includes contracts outside the W0 cohort, which enter the data only through approvals from cohort contracts.

This has two consequences. First, for a depth-one spender the walk does nothing but reweight its approving owners: an approval weighs more when it is recent and large, up to a weight of one, and less when its owner spreads its approvals over many spenders. Apart from these weights and this division, EndorseRank and the count carry the same information about such a spender, and there is nothing further for propagation to supply. We did not isolate which of the weights costs EndorseRank its agreement with later approvals. Second, longer paths exist. Roughly one cohort spender in six at $\Tobs$, and one W0 spender in three, is approved by an owner that others approve in turn, and most of these scores differ from the closed form by more than 1\%. Propagation over several steps therefore occurs in these graphs; it did not, however, lift EndorseRank above the raw count out of window, with uniform or with activity restarts. AWP, which walks a transfer graph with cycles, has no comparable closed form.

\textit{Counts (R1 holds).} Among the W1 traders the highest in-approve degree is one, so P in effect compares the 37 traders that had received an approval with the 33 that had not. The in-approve degree ranks the later LFCR at $\tau=0.394$ $[0.265,0.518]$ and the transfer in-degree at $0.253$ $[0.117,0.379]$, so the transfer count also ranks this outcome. P is $+0.141$ $[0.037,0.240]$, with a 97.5\% interval of $[0.026,0.256]$ that lies above zero, and $+0.145$ $[0.040,0.328]$ stratified by the number of closes. W0 gives $\mathrm{P}=+0.095$ (97.5\% interval $[-0.041,0.263]$), positive as R1 requires but not resolved. All three conditions of R1 hold, and the registered wording for this case applies: the approval count at the freeze ranked contract traders above the transfer count on later liquidation avoidance. The scores were defined after the registered results were known, so this verdict is a re-analysis and not the outcome of a registered test; in the registered analysis R1 did not hold (Table~\ref{tab6}).

\textit{PageRanks (R2 does not hold).} Q, EndorseRank with activity restarts minus AWP, is $+0.023$ in W1 (97.5\% interval $[-0.071,0.127]$) and $-0.012$ in W0 (97.5\% interval $[-0.177,0.168]$). In the registered wording, the PageRank versions are not resolved. The 97.5\% interval of Q in W1 is 0.20 wide, so at these sample sizes an estimate of 0.1 or less, the size of every degree contrast on the spender labels (Table~\ref{tab3}), would not have been resolved. The other pairs are not resolved either: EndorseRank minus AWP is $+0.034$ $[-0.067,0.134]$ in W1 and $-0.019$ $[-0.173,0.144]$ in W0, and the amount-weighted layers differ by $+0.019$ $[-0.093,0.128]$ and $-0.057$ $[-0.209,0.092]$. In a contrast that the registration document did not name, EndorseRank falls below the approval count in both windows, by $-0.097$ $[-0.174,-0.009]$ in W1 and $-0.109$ $[-0.196,-0.018]$ in W0. Here, as on the spender labels, the walk with uniform restarts loses to the count it smooths.

\textit{The other labels (R3 applies).} The two shares that do not grow with trading run the other way. In W1 the transfer count ranks traders above the approval count on both shares, with P at $\dt=-0.162$ $[-0.295,-0.025]$ for the profitable share and $-0.222$ $[-0.328,-0.106]$ for the non-loss share. R3 therefore applies, and the registered wording reads: the signal concerns forced-liquidation avoidance, not trading success. A liquidated close counts as not losing, so some of the gap on the non-loss share follows from the definition; the profitable share counts such a close as not profitable, and R3 rests mainly on that share. On the no-liquidation flag P is $+0.141$ $[0.044,0.232]$ in W1 and $+0.109$ $[-0.022,0.257]$ in W0. On the two outcomes that grow with trading, the PageRank pairs favor the transfer side in W1: Q is $-0.215$ $[-0.399,-0.042]$ on profitable closes and $-0.299$ $[-0.457,-0.146]$ on realized gain, where AWP reaches $0.280$ $[0.111,0.435]$. \textit{Who the recipients are.} None of the recipients was liquidated in either window (37 of 37 in W1, 39 of 39 in W0), whereas 72.7\% and 75.0\% of the other traders went without a liquidation (Table~\ref{tab5}). Recipients were not simply less active: they closed more positions (median 24 against 11 in W1 and 30 against 10 in W0) and had lower mean profitable and non-loss shares (0.325 against 0.479 and 0.433 against 0.644 in W1), the pattern behind R3. Dropping the ten recipients with the most approving owners leaves P at $+0.155$ $[0.032,0.276]$ in W1 and $+0.088$ $[-0.048,0.240]$ in W0; with nearly all degrees equal to one, the ten dropped are taken in node order. All traders in both windows are contracts, so the split into recipients and others is not a split by account type. One explanation would fit every row of Table~\ref{tab5}: recipients may be vault or managed-trading contracts that others authorize to move their tokens, that trade at low leverage and adjust positions often, and so are rarely liquidated, close many partial positions and earn modest profitable shares. The data hold neither leverage nor the role of each contract, so this explanation is untested.

\subsection*{The registered analysis}

The registered analysis, with raw base units over every ERC-20 token, scores from every event since 1~October~2023 and the plan's cohort of 27,844 contracts, reached the same verdicts on R2 and R3 but not on R1 (Table~\ref{tab6}). There, P in W1 was $+0.063$ $[-0.026,0.148]$ with a 97.5\% interval of $[-0.040,0.158]$, and its stratified interval also included zero; Q in W1 was $+0.051$ with a 97.5\% interval of $[-0.104,0.232]$; R1 and R2 did not hold, and R3 applied. These are its registered results. The count-level lead of the revised analysis is therefore the one verdict on which the two analyses differ, and only the registered verdict is the outcome of a test fixed before this study extracted the data it judges. The two analyses also differ on two degree contrasts, which no rule decides. In the registered analysis AWP rose above the transfer in-degree in both windows ($+0.038$ $[0.035,0.042]$ and $+0.020$ $[0.016,0.023]$), and the activity variant rose above the in-approve degree, each with an interval that excludes zero; in the revised analysis both fall below their counts. EndorseRank fell below the in-approve degree in both analyses and met the closed form for every depth-one spender in both. On the liquidation-free close rate the allowance-against-transfer PageRank pairs, Q, EndorseRank minus AWP and the amount-weighted layers, were positive in both windows of the registered analysis; in the revised analysis they are positive in W1 and negative in W0, all with intervals that include zero (Table~\ref{tab6}).

\subsection*{Computational cost}

With one solver and identical settings, EndorseRank's solver graph (3,808,949 edges on 2,513,982 nodes) took 2.66\,s on average and AWP's (8,426,124 edges on 3,601,727 nodes) 8.53\,s, over five timed runs with standard deviations of 0.11 and 0.62\,s. AWP thus took 3.21 times as long at an edge ratio of 2.21; it also needed more iterations (94 against 57), and its peak memory was 663.7\,MB against 325.3\,MB. Matrix assembly and each power iteration are linear in the number of edges~\cite{leskovec2020mining}, so the difference in time follows from the size of the transfer graph and from the iterations the walk needs on it, which the benchmark does not separate, and not from any property of the algorithm. Any walk that also uses the transfer edges pays for them: the companion's mixed walk over both edge sets (10,562,390 edges) took 11.56\,s.

%======================================================================
\section*{Discussion}

\subsection*{The edge type sets which later arrivals a score ranks; neither walk beat its raw degree}

The two edge types measure different things, and the out-of-window results show it in both windows: scores built on allowances rank which contracts later gain new approvals, and scores built on transfers which later gain new senders. Choosing the edge is therefore a decision about what a reputation score for contracts is meant to follow. Propagating along the chosen edge added nothing on either side. In comparisons made after the labels were known, AWP fell below the transfer count and EndorseRank below the approval count in both windows, and on the restricted set of spenders that had received a transfer the same held in W0. That a count is hard to beat is unsurprising given preferential attachment and link-prediction practice~\cite{barabasi1999scaling,libennowell2007link}, but on-chain reputation work rarely tests it, comparing walks with each other or with statistics of their own edges~\cite{do2023awp}.

The closed form says what EndorseRank computes for most spenders: the approval count, with each approval scaled by how recent and how large it is and then divided by its owner's total approval weight. That normalization lowers a spender whose owners approve many other contracts; whether it, or the recency and value weights, cost EndorseRank its agreement with later approvals was not isolated. The variant with activity restarts, which sends restart mass to the owners that approve most, ranked later approval pairs above EndorseRank in both windows but still below the count (Table~\ref{tab3}), so in these comparisons, all made after the labels were known, the restarts at active owners narrowed the gap to the count without closing it. AWP was run only with its published restarts, and it fell short as well. Whether propagation adds to the count where a walk is more than a reweighted count would need a sample extracted two or more hops out and a registered test on a window not yet extracted, reporting spenders of depth one, where the walk reduces to a weighted count, separately from deeper spenders, where propagation can matter.

\subsection*{What the trader comparison shows}

The trader outcomes are recorded by the exchange and not by either graph, and they were the only outcomes in these data that neither graph is built from, although GMX payouts made before the freeze can appear in the transfer graph. On the primary outcome the approval count separated from the transfer count in this re-analysis. In W1 the approval count ranked later liquidation avoidance at $\tau=0.394$ $[0.265,0.518]$ and the transfer count at $0.253$ $[0.117,0.379]$, and the difference between them, P, had a 97.5\% interval above zero, as did P stratified by the number of closes. In W0, the secondary window, whose label window lies inside W1's score window, P was positive with a 97.5\% interval that reached below zero; R1 asked only for a positive estimate there. Two facts bound this result. The scores were defined after the registered results were known, and in the registered analysis P in W1 had a 97.5\% interval that reached below zero, so the lead is a finding of the re-analysis and not of a registered test. And the lead rests on 37 approval recipients against 33 other traders, all of them contracts. The PageRank pair was not resolved in either window of either analysis (Table~\ref{tab6}). On the outcomes of trading success the transfer side led wherever a difference between an allowance-side and a transfer-side score was resolved, and no score ranked the profitable share with an interval above zero in either window.

Beyond the rule, the pattern is descriptive: no recipient contract was liquidated in either window. That pattern rests on a few dozen contracts, may reflect what those contracts are rather than who approved them, and was not compared with what a venue already knows before the freeze, such as a contract's own liquidation record, its number of closes or its leverage. It does not show value beyond past behavior, and nothing here suggests that approvals measure creditworthiness, default risk or trading skill. Whether an approval count could help a margin or lending venue screen contract counterparties remains open; it would need a registered test on a window not yet extracted and on more contract traders, with past behavior controlled.

\subsection*{Implications for evaluating on-chain reputation}

The study suggests four practices for evaluating on-chain reputation scores. First, report the raw counts beside every walk: here neither walk beat its count out of window, which a walk checked only against statistics of its own edges~\cite{do2023awp} could not have shown. Second, freeze scores before any label is counted. Third, compare edge types on outcomes that neither was built from, since each leads on the labels of its own construct by design~\cite{cronbach1955construct}, and check how separate those outcomes are. Fourth, state for every comparison when it was fixed relative to the data, and set an analysis defined after the results were known beside the registered one~\cite{nosek2018preregistration}. Here the two analyses agreed on R2 and R3, but the count-level lead on liquidation avoidance holds only in the analysis defined afterwards, and the leads of AWP and of the activity variant over their counts appear only in the registered one.

\subsection*{Practical implications}

An owner deciding whether to approve a contract could be shown how many distinct owners already hold a positive allowance to it, a public number that wallet software can compute; out of window, EndorseRank ranked later new approval pairs below that number, with uniform or with activity restarts. Such a count tells an owner how widely a contract is already authorized, not what the contract will do with an allowance: a phishing contract gains approvals as an honest router does, and a new contract scores low whatever its code. A low count is a reason to look closer, and a high count is no reason to sign. A raw count of distinct owners is also cheap to inflate, since approvals from $N$ fresh addresses raise it by $N$ for $N$ transaction fees with no tokens locked, and a uniformly restarted PageRank is open to farms of addresses that approve one another~\cite{gyongyi2005alliances,cheng2005sybilproof}; the companion manuscript quantifies that exposure. For ranking which contracts will gain new transfer senders, the count of distinct senders likewise ranked above AWP in both windows (Table~\ref{tab3}), in comparisons made after the labels were known. None of these scores is a security audit or a credit score, and none replaces collateral~\cite{gudgeon2020crisis}.

\subsection*{Limitations}

The evidence comes from one chain, score windows of twelve months and two three-month label windows, so other rollups and Layer-1 networks would need new data~\cite{werner2022sok}. The graphs keep five tokens, so contracts that owners approve only on other tokens are outside the cohort, and native ether enters only as WETH. Approvals older than the score window are not read even when they are still in force, so a contract that owners authorized long ago and have not authorized again scores as if it had fewer owners. Both graphs are ego networks of one cohort of contracts, so owners' out-strengths, senders' activeness and the paths a walk can take are those of that network and not of the chain, and the finding about propagation does not carry over to graphs with longer endorsement paths. The revised analysis was defined after the registered results were known, so its tokens, price source, slopes, cap and score windows were all chosen by people who had seen those results. Its constants come from the W0 score window, so no label enters them, and the registered analysis reached the same verdicts on R2 and R3; it did not meet R1, so the count-level lead rests on the analysis defined afterwards. AWP's parameters are our choices, as its paper gives none. The spender labels are sparse counts of arrivals, which favor any score that tracks the current number of counterparties. Every interval treats contracts as independent and the graphs as fixed, although spenders share owners, so the intervals are probably too narrow; the spender analyses use only 400 resamples, and only the decision pair is adjusted for multiplicity. Account type was read at blocks after both label windows, and a contract that destroyed itself before that read counts as an externally owned account and drops out. An \texttt{Approval} event can record the remainder after a spend as well as a grant, and allowances inside managers such as Permit2 are unseen. The trader cohorts are small, the trader labels count partial closes, and market conditions, which drive liquidations, were not measured. No default labels from unsecured lending were available, and no causal claim is made.

%======================================================================
\section*{Conclusions}

Allowance edges and transfer edges carry different information about the same smart contracts. On Arbitrum One, scores built on the latest allowances ranked which contracts would gain new approvals, and scores built on transfers which would gain new senders. Neither walk improved on the raw degree it smooths: in comparisons made once the labels were known, AWP placed the contracts that went on to gain new senders below the transfer in-degree in both windows, and EndorseRank placed those that went on to gain approval pairs below the count of approving owners in both, with uniform or with activity restarts; for most spenders it is a reweighted approval count, as its closed form shows. On an outcome that neither graph contains, the later liquidation avoidance of contract traders, the approval count ranked traders above the transfer count in the primary window, which meets the registered rule for a count-level lead in this re-analysis but did not in the registered analysis; the PageRank versions were not resolved in either analysis. The next step is a registered test of that count-level lead on a window not yet extracted, with more contract traders and their past liquidations controlled, and any further test of the walks should report depth-one and deeper spenders separately.
